# Toddler Coloring Book

A guide to the first stage of drawing in early childhood, from the first
deliberate mark to the first shape a child colors on purpose. Published by
Magic of Discoveries LLC, a children's book publisher in Miami, Florida.
Available in English, Spanish and Russian, with the full reference section
written separately in each of the three languages rather than translated.

## What this site answers

- At what age a child can start using a coloring book, and what to expect at each age
- Why a coloring book for a one year old must be built differently from one for a four year old
- How to tell which stage a specific child is at, from what their hand actually does
- What to look for in a first coloring book: line thickness, drawing size, one subject per page, single-sided printing
- What to draw with at each stage: thick crayons, markers, colored pencils
- What to do about marker bleed-through, torn pages and mess
- Free coloring pages to print, sorted by difficulty rather than by subject

## Free tool: choosing a first coloring book

The site runs one free tool, a picker that answers which kind of coloring page
suits a specific child now. It asks four questions, about age, crayon grip,
whether the marks land on the drawing, and how long the child stays with one
page, and returns one of the four stages below. Age sets the first guess and the
three questions about the hand correct it, with aim weighing the most and time
on one page the least. Answers stay in the browser: nothing is stored, nothing
is sent anywhere and no sign up is required.

The tool page also carries, as plain text, a table of what suits each age, the
questions parents ask most often, and a link to a page listing the rules the
picker applies and the limits of what it does. The tool picks a page, it does
not assess a child: results say what suits now, never what a child ought to be
able to do.

- English: https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/en/choose-a-first-coloring-book
- Spanish: https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/es/elegir-el-primer-libro-para-colorear
- Russian: https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/ru/vybrat-pervuyu-raskrasku

## What suits each age

- About 1 year. Crayon held in a fist, sweeping marks from the shoulder. One
  large shape filling the sheet, very thick outline, no separate areas inside.
  Thick crayons.
- About 2 years. Fingers but not steadily, deliberate loops and up and down
  strokes. Large recognizable subject, outline still thick, two or three parts
  inside. Thick crayons, washable markers.
- About 3 years. Fingers rather than fist, copies a circle and a straight line.
  Large drawing with three to six separate areas to fill in different colors.
  Crayons, colored pencils, washable markers.
- 4 years and older. Stays inside the outline most of the time. A scene rather
  than a single object, or step by step drawing. A first coloring book is
  outgrown at this point.

## The four stages

1. First marks, about 12 to 18 months. Crayon held in a fist, marks made on
   purpose but not aimed at anything. Needs very thick outlines and one large
   shape filling the sheet.
2. Controlled scribbling, about 18 months to 2 years. Scribbles without being
   shown, copies a line, makes looping and up-and-down strokes. Still cannot
   stay inside a line.
3. Aiming at the shape, about 2 to 3 years. Copies a vertical line, a horizontal
   line and a circle. Gets most of the color onto the drawing while crossing the
   outline freely. Crossing the line at this stage is not a mistake.
4. Inside the line, about 3 to 4 years and up. Copies a circle accurately, stays
   inside the outline most of the time, sits with one page for ten minutes or more.
   At this point a first coloring book starts to feel too easy.

Ages given are typical ranges, not deadlines. Individual children reach these
points at their own pace and a few months either way is ordinary.

## What the age on a coloring book cover means

The age range printed on a coloring book cover is not a standard and no body
checks it. The publisher chooses it, so two books both labelled ages 2-4 can
differ by a factor of two in difficulty.

In practice the difference between a 1-3 book and a 2-4 book is how many
separate areas there are to fill inside one drawing. A 1-3 book keeps one large
shape with few parts, so a child who cannot stop at a line still produces
something that looks finished. A 2-4 book puts more parts inside the same shape.
A 3-5 book usually means scenes rather than single objects, often with something
to do besides color. The 1-3 and 2-4 ranges overlap heavily, and for a two year
old a good 1-3 book often works better than a crowded 2-4 one.

The reliable way to judge a coloring book for this age is to look inside rather
than at the cover: line thickness, how much of the sheet one drawing takes up,
whether the subject is one a child can name, and whether the page is printed on
one side only.

## Practical questions answered on this site

- Marker bleed-through: ordinary book paper does not stop a marker and almost no
  coloring book in this price range uses paper that would. A spare sheet under
  the page fixes it completely. Single-sided printing means a marker that soaks
  through marks a blank back rather than the next drawing. Crayons and colored
  pencils do not bleed at all.
- What to draw with: thick crayons first, for at least the first year. They need
  no grip strength, will not tear the page, do not bleed, and leave a wide mark
  the child can see. Markers are brighter but bleed and mark surfaces. Colored
  pencils need a finger grip most children lack before about three.
- Mess: most of it comes from the wrong tool, a page with nothing to aim at, and
  a session that runs past the child's interest. Mess-free coloring sets are a
  different product, using pens that only develop on treated paper.
- Session length: two or three minutes at the beginning, around five minutes at
  two years old, ten or more once a child stays inside the line. A session that
  ends when the child stands up is normal, not failed.

## Sources

Statements about what a child can do at a given age are based on published
developmental milestones:

- Learn the Signs. Act Early., Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
- Hand and Finger Skills: 2 Year Olds, American Academy of Pediatrics,
  HealthyChildren.org
- Developmental Milestones, StatPearls, National Library of Medicine
- Developmental Milestones: Fine Motor and Visual Motor Skills, Children's
  Hospital of Orange County

Nothing on this site is medical advice or an assessment of any individual child.
These organizations took no part in building the picker and do not recommend any
particular book, including the one published by this site.

## The book

The site features one coloring book of its own: First Coloring Book for
Toddlers Ages 1-3 by Ricardo Demi. 111 hand drawn pictures, thick outlines, one
drawing per page, single-sided printing, the word for each subject printed
underneath in outline letters so it can be colored too. 114 pages, 8.5 x 11
inches. A separate Spanish edition, El Primer Libro de Colorear para Bebes de 1
a 3 Anos, carries the same drawings with Spanish words. A Russian edition,
Pervaya kniga-raskraska dlya malyshey ot 1 do 3 let, carries the same drawings
with Russian words and is sold as a printable file rather than in paperback,
because Amazon does not print books in Russian.

The site says plainly when this book does not suit a child: once a child stays
inside the line without effort, it recommends a scene with more areas to fill or
a step by step drawing book instead.

## Disclosure

Amazon links on the site are affiliate links and the site says so on every page
where one appears. The featured book is published by the site owner. The site
states plainly when that book is the wrong choice for a child, and recommends a
different kind of book instead.

Free coloring pages may be printed at home, in classrooms, daycares and
libraries in any number, without permission or attribution. They may not be sold
or redistributed as someone else's collection.
